summary:
Shadow Self is a health-monitoring engine and dashboard for astronauts on long missions to the Moon and Mars.

Each astronaut gets a “shadow self”, a personal model that predicts what their heart rate and heart rate variability should be from their sleep, workload, and cabin CO2. When real readings drift away from that prediction, Shadow Self notices early, before a fixed alarm threshold would. It checks five systems: radiation, muscle, bone, eyes and brain (SANS), and heart. It turns those checks into daily 0–100 scores, a short action plan for the crew, and a summary for mission control on Earth. It also tracks solar flares, proton events, and geomagnetic storms using NOAA space weather data, and adjusts radiation levels for the ISS, the Moon, or Mars.

On 10 simulated 30-day missions, it caught 100% of injected health events and slow drifts, averaging 0.2 false alarms per mission. Across 61 automated missions, it flagged problems about 38 days before they crossed a danger threshold.

Far from Earth, help is days away. Shadow Self gives crews and doctors warning early enough to act.
details:
What it does

Shadow Self is a health-monitoring engine and dashboard for astronauts on long missions. The main idea is a shadow self, which is a personal model for each astronaut that learns what is normal for them. From each day’s sleep, workload, and cabin CO2, it predicts what their resting heart rate and heart rate variability should be. When real readings keep drifting away from that prediction, Shadow Self flags it early, often days or weeks before a fixed danger threshold would.

The inner workings

  1. Ingestion: sensor streams, daily logs and periodic tests are loaded into a SQLite database in batches, so even million-row missions use about 55 MB of memory
  2. Fast checks: every 5 seconds, it checks heartbeat and radiation for emergencies
  3. Five body-system modules: radiation, muscle, bone, eyes and brain (SANS), and heart. The heart module uses CUSUM drift detection on the shadow self’s prediction errors to catch slow changes
  4. Fusion: it combines the modules into a daily 0–100 score per system, with Watch, Act, and Urgent zones, plus hard safety rules
  5. Actions: it writes a short ranked plan for the crew (at most 3 actions), alerts, and a summary for mission control
  6. Space weather: it reads NOAA data on solar flares, proton events, and geomagnetic storms and gives early watch, warning, and critical alerts so crews can shelter
  7. Radiation budget: it tracks each astronaut’s dose against NASA-STD-3001’s 600 mSv career limit, including dose from earlier flights
  8. Environment profiles: the background radiation changes for ISS, Moon, or Mars missions

Benefits, Impact, and the Good stuff

On Mars, messages take up to 20 minutes each way and help is months away, so crews need to catch problems themselves. Shadow Self gives early, personal warnings and plain-language next steps instead of raw numbers. In testing on 10 simulated 30-day missions, it caught 100% of injected health events and slow drifts, averaging 0.2 false alarms per mission. Across 61 automated missions, it flagged problems about 38 days before they crossed a danger threshold. We changed the settings on some missions and tested on missions it had never seen.

Creativity?

  • Instead of one alarm level for everyone, each astronaut is compared to their own predicted self
  • Body health and space weather are combined in one view
  • Every module has a safe fallback, so one crashed system never stops the others
  • An AI assistant explains results in plain English and still works offline with simple rules when there’s no internet, just like on a real spacecraft

Tools and languages and resources

Python (engine, simulator, scoring), SQLite, PyTorch (an experimental neural “Shadow Net” heart model), HTML/CSS/JavaScript (dashboard website), the Groq API (AI assistant), NOAA SWPC data feeds, Git/GitHub, and IDLE/VS Code. We also used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant.

Considerations we took

  • False alarms vs. early warning: too many alarms and astronauts start ignoring them, so we compared several score cutoffs
  • Honest testing: we don’t have real astronaut data, so we built a simulator with a hidden answer key and scored our engine against it
  • Memory and speed for long missions
  • Clear wording for tired crews
  • NASA’s real radiation limits
